Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez (Redwood) — Lena Park, Omar Farouk, Priya Menon (Cerulean Payments)
summary: Intro demo of Redwood Hosted API focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff and idempotency, basic cost/latency tradeoffs. Customer is evaluating for conversational payment support and fraud triage; interested in trial and security docs.
transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Diego from our solutions engineering team is with me. 
00:08 Priya Menon: Hi Maya, thanks, we have about 40 minutes. Lena and Omar here as well. We're interested in your hosted API for chat use cases — es- essentially customer support + some payment dispute triage.
00:18 Diego Alvarez: Great, yeah we'll walk through the hosted API flow for chat/text generation, show streaming, important params, and how retries work. We'll also highlight security controls.
02:05 Maya Chen: Before we start quick qual — what's your current stack? Are you using OpenAI or self-hosted models today?
02:15 Lena Park: We're currently running a mix — quick prototypes on OpenAI for NLU and some homegrown rules. We want predictable latency and cost; spikes during batch dispute windows are painful.
02:30 Omar Farouk: Also infra constraints — most of our traffic is in us-east, but we need EU data residency for a subset of merchants.
03:05 Diego Alvarez: Makes sense. Redwood hosted API can route regionally; you can pin models and also use routing policies for residency. We'll show that in the console later — but for today demo we'll focus on the API behaviors.
04:10 Diego Alvarez: (screen share) Ok here's the basic call — POST /v1/chat/completions, payload includes messages array, model name, streaming flag. If you set stream: true we send events over SSE, so clients can render partial tokens.
05:03 Lena Park: How does streaming affect cost? Is it more expensive?
05:12 Diego Alvarez: Cost is per output token regardless of streaming; streaming just changes delivery. However, latency SLOs differ — streaming reduces time-to-first-token which helps perceived latency.
06:00 Priya Menon: What about retries? We need idempotent retry logic for webhook-style flows.
06:12 Diego Alvarez: Right — Redwood recommends using a request_id in metadata and an idempotency_key header for any non-idempotent writes. Retries on transient 5xx or network failures use exponential backoff; client libraries include helpers.
07:00 Omar Farouk: Do you expose a retry-after header or backoff guidance?
07:10 Diego Alvarez: We send standard Retry-After on rate limits and include a x-redwood-retry-code in some cases. For most cases exponential backoff starting at 500ms with jitter works well.
08:05 Maya Chen: Quick note on params — temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling. For deterministic outputs you set temperature to 0 and often lower max_tokens. We demo prompt templates too.
09:04 Diego Alvarez: (demo live code snippet) Example: {"model":"redwood-1-s", "messages": [...], "stream": true, "temperature":0.2, "max_tokens":256} and we show SSE events like data: {"token":"Please"} etc.
11:30 Lena Park: Any support for function/tool calling or structured JSON outputs? We need to return structured decisions for downstream services.
11:40 Diego Alvarez: Yes — we support function calling and structured output via JSON schema enforcement; model will return parsed JSON or a function call object you can execute.
13:00 Priya Menon: On security — SOC 2, SSO, KMS — what do you provide?
13:15 Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II, SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC, and you can bring your own KMS in Private deployments. Hosted supports customer-managed keys via cloud KMS integrations for encryption at rest; detailed docs in the security pack.
14:20 Omar Farouk: Data retention — can you short-retain transcripts or opt out of training?
14:30 Maya Chen: Hosted API has configurable retention; by default we retain for operational reasons but you can opt out of model training and set retention windows. We'll send the exact retention policy.
15:40 Diego Alvarez: Back to retries — also watch for streaming connection interruptions: if a stream drops mid-response you get a partial completion id; with the same idempotency_key the service can decide to resume or re-run safely.
17:05 Lena Park: How about throughput — we're targeting 100 qps during peak with 512 token contexts. Any guidance on cost and latency?
17:20 Diego Alvarez: For 100 qps with 512 tokens, we recommend batchers and batching settings; on hosted we can provision capacity. I can run a cost estimate — roughly X tokens * price, but I'll send a spreadsheet after the call.
19:40 Priya Menon: You mentioned model variants — does Redwood auto-fallback to cheaper models if capacity is constrained?
19:52 Diego Alvarez: Yes, routing policies can fallback to compatible model variants (lower-cost or quantized) with automatic degrading rules; you can also do A/B split.
21:10 Omar Farouk: Latency SLOs per token?
21:20 Diego Alvarez: It depends on model and region; for redwood-1-s in us-east we typically see 30-80ms first token and 10-20ms per token after, but we'll include measured percentiles.
23:00 Lena Park: We need compliance docs and an attack surface review for our security team.
23:10 Maya Chen: We'll attach SOC2, ISO summary, network diagrams, and a short security FAQ — sending after this meeting.
24:05 Diego Alvarez: Demoing console briefly — here's the per-route dashboards, streaming logs, and cost breakdown by token type. You can set per-key quotas.
26:30 Priya Menon: How do you handle billing — per-token or subscription? Our finance team wants predictability.
26:40 Maya Chen: Hosted is usage-based per output/input token. For predictable cost we have committed reserved (Dedicated) options and monthly commits. We'll include both pricing scenarios in the sheet.
28:12 Omar Farouk: Any SDKs? Node, Python?
28:18 Diego Alvarez: Yes official SDKs for Node/Python/Go with built-in streaming helpers and retries.
29:20 Lena Park: Do you support low-latency websocket streams or only SSE?
29:30 Diego Alvarez: We support SSE for browser-friendly streaming and websockets for persistent connections; SDK abstracts both.
31:05 Priya Menon: For trial access can we get an API key scoped to a test environment?
31:15 Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll provision a trial key with quotas and sample prompt buckets; Diego will set up a sample benchmark harness.
33:00 Diego Alvarez: One more note: caching — you can enable prefix/KV caching at the request level to reduce cost for repeated prompts. Helpful for FAQ-like flows.
34:05 Lena Park: That could help a lot. For dispute triage we have common templates.
34:20 Diego Alvarez: Also Optimize suggestions — the Optimize product will recommend batching configs and quantization to hit target latency/cost. We can run an Optimize analysis during the PoC.
36:10 Priya Menon: Ok let's recap next steps.
36:20 Maya Chen: Recap: I will send pricing, SOC2/security pack, and trial onboarding doc. Diego will run the latency/cost estimate and set up a benchmark session. Lena will share sample transcripts. We agreed to reconvene week of 3/9 for a deeper benchmark.
37:05 Omar Farouk: Sounds good — one ask: can you include a simple sample showing idempotency headers usage in the SDK?
37:12 Diego Alvarez: Yes I'll add that to the trial repo.
38:00 Priya Menon: Any blockers?
38:06 Lena Park: Mostly procurement questions around data residency and encryption which look addressable.
38:20 Maya Chen: Great, we'll follow up — thanks everyone.
38:30 Meeting end
notes: Call had typical transcription garbling: some product names like 'Redwood Optimize' transcribed as 'Redwood Optimise' in places; speakers overlapped a bit. Customer is high priority (payment vertical) — good chance to convert to trial and then dedicated capacity if benchmarks look good.
